question: The European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Destroying Videogames’ has collected over 1.2 million signatures from EU citizens. The breadth of support shows that this issue is important to players, i.e. European consumers. Videogames are not just a form of entertainment nowadays; they play an important role in education, socialisation, culture and sport.

The largest AAA productions cost up to EUR 60– 70 on the day of their release. However, many games are designed in such a way that they cease to function after technical support provided by the producer ends, regardless of whether or not the consumer has purchased the game.

This raises serious legal and ethical questions: can consumers be prevented from using a purchased product solely because the producer considered it unprofitable to maintain this product, and should rules not be adopted stating that it is consumers who have the right to decide when to stop using a product they have purchased, rather than the person who produced the product?
These practices also raise questions in the context of the European circular economy policy, which aims to combat waste and planned obsolescence. In light of the above:
Is the Commission considering drawing up realistic and enforceable regulations in relation to this issue?
Is the Commission also considering addressing price differences on the European gaming market, including higher prices in countries such as Poland?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.4.2026) The European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) ‘Stop Destroying Video games’ was submitted to the Commission on 26 January 2026. On 23 February 2026, the Commission met with the ECI organisers to enable them to present the objectives of the initiative in detail, clarify its requests and provide further background information.

By July 2026, the Commission will adopt a formal reply, in the form of a communication, setting out its conclusions on the initiative and the measures, if any, it intends to take. As regards the substantive issues raised by the ECI, the Commission refers to its previous reply to written question E-003581/2025.
The ECI does not concern price differences for video games in the EU, and this matter is not being addressed by the Commission in the context of its reply to the ECI.

EU consumer legislation, in particular, the Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU1 requires traders, including video game providers, to provide consumers with information about the total price of their offers but it does not regulate the level of prices. Copyright-protected services, such as video games, are not covered by the principle of non-discrimination under the Geoblocking Regulation (EU) 2018/3022.

However, other rules in the Regulation, such as on blocking access to online interfaces or re-routing without the customer's prior consent as well as discrimination for reasons related to payment, apply.
